subject: random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
parts:
Hi all.

Attached are two examples of using random Fourier features
[Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximate Gaussian process regression.
The idea is that the covariance matrix is approximated by an explicit
randomized feature expansion of the kernel. With an explicit feature
space expansion, there's no costly multivariate matrix algebra--it
just becomes Bayesian linear regression on the new features.

In rff1.stan, I don't learn the lengthscale and it's very fast for
1000 data points. In rff2.stan, I do learn the lengthscale and it's
pretty slow (10 minutes), though it can still handle 1000 data points
with a small number of features. (Note that in the attached I only
have 10 features, but in real applications people often use 10K-100K
features!)

Anyone have thoughts on speeding up rff2.stan? My guess is that
there'd be a big speedup from a vectorized sin/cos, with analytic
gradients. If that sounds right, I'll file a feature request and
hopefully Rob and I can tackle this (+ anyone else who wants to help).

Seth

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
parts:
We'll have all the unary functions vectorized soon, but there
won't be any speedup over loops because there are no shared
computations. We might be able to get fancier with the implementation
and cut down some virtual function calls, but that's minor compared
to shared computations.

But you can speed up this loop:

for(i in 1:n)
for(j in 1:k) {
cosfeatures[i,j] = scale * cos(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
sinfeatures[i,j] = scale * sin(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
}

Define the I x J matrix of omega * x, then multpily it by bw,
then use it to define cosfeatures and sinfeatures without the
scale, then multiply through by the scale.

The target+= forms of the densities are slower than the
~ forms because they don't drop constant terms (yes, yes, versions
that do drop constants are on my to-do list buried somewhere I
might get to them next year if I'm lucky).

With transformed data now, different RNGs get used per chain.
I'm going to fix that for the next release.

It'll also be faster if you only save fhat as a transformed parameter
and use that in the last normal_lpdf --- less I/O per iteration (reduces
n x k to n) and also saves some redundant calculations in generated
quantities.

sqrt(2.0 / n) rather than sqrt(2 / (1.0 * n)) just for clarity.

- Bob

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
parts:
Thanks for all the suggestions! (Down to 8 minutes, and more than
twice as many effective samples.) Updated versions attached.

1) Moving the random number generation to R instead of transformed
data is important as there's now much better convergence of the
different chains, which makes sense since they're actually using the
same features now. But before you go and fix this, might be worth
seeing what other people use it for...I could imagine the current
behavior of different seeds for transformed data making sense in some
cases.

2) OK, good to hear about unary function vectorization. I guess I was
hoping that analytic gradients would make a big difference in terms of
the shared computations you're talking about. Consider n = 1 so we
have a real x, a parameter bw we want to learn, and omega is a vector
of size k. If sin(.) was vectorized, then we'd have:

sinfeatures = sin(omega * bw * x);

and the gradient with respect to x would be:

(omega * bw) .* cos(omega * bw * x)

i.e. elementwise product of two vectors. (For n > 1 it's elementwise
product of two matrices.) Won't that be faster since omega * bw will
only need to be calculated once?

Seth

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
parts:
Bochner's theorem says any stationary kernel has a spectral
representation that's a probability measure--the kernel is the Fourier
transform of the spectral measure. So the idea is to approximate the
kernel, which is an integral, you use Monte Carlo samples from the
spectral measure. For a Gaussian kernel, the corresponding spectral
representation is also a Gaussian, so you sample the Fourier
frequencies (hence the sin/cos) from a Gaussian distribution. Once you
have the features, you can learn the coefficients for them, i.e.
Bayesian linear regression. People have generalized it to
non-stationary kernels, have shown how to get lower variance with
quasi-Monte Carlo, and have computational tricks for when you need
100K features for large n datasets.

A related idea is Sparse Spectrum GPs [Lázaro-Gredilla et al 2010], in
which instead of fixing the frequencies you optimize them (but fix the
coefficients) and thus learn a new kernel. I'm not aware of anyone
trying to learn a posterior over the frequencies by putting a prior on
them and sampling, but that might be a nice way of getting a Bayesian
non-parametric kernel. Or it might be very unidentifiable...

...but I'm not sure what a KL expansion of the GP would be...maybe
there's a connection?
Seth

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
parts:
It would be, but you're talking about an analytic gradient
for a compound expression.

> On Sep 12, 2016, at 11:19 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for all the suggestions! (Down to 8 minutes, and more than
> twice as many effective samples.) Updated versions attached.
>

> data is important as there's now much better convergence of the
> different chains, which makes sense since they're actually using the
> same features now. But before you go and fix this, might be worth
> seeing what other people use it for...I could imagine the current
> behavior of different seeds for transformed data making sense in some
> cases.

I am going to fix it. We decided a couple meetings ago.

There are two arguments, seed and chain ID. Seed will control
how transformed data goes and chain ID how the rest goes. So you
will still be able to get different results by changing the seed.

> 2) OK, good to hear about unary function vectorization. I guess I was
> hoping that analytic gradients would make a big difference in terms of
> the shared computations you're talking about. Consider n = 1 so we
> have a real x, a parameter bw we want to learn, and omega is a vector
> of size k. If sin(.) was vectorized, then we'd have:
>
> sinfeatures = sin(omega * bw * x);
>
> and the gradient with respect to x would be:
>
> (omega * bw) .* cos(omega * bw * x)
>
> i.e. elementwise product of two vectors. (For n > 1 it's elementwise
> product of two matrices.) Won't that be faster since omega * bw will
> only need to be calculated once?

That'd be faster if we could somehow be this clever on the algebra.
But that's not how autodiff works. It just blindly plugs the
chain rule through element by element.

We'll eventually figure out a way to get user-defined analytic gradients,
or when there are reusable special functions, we can plumb analytic
gradients through.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random Fourier features for Gaussian process regression
parts:
I just put it up as a repo:
https://bitbucket.org/flaxter/random-fourier-features-in-stan

Seth

On Tue, Sep 13, 2016 at 12:34 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Mind posting the updated code? (possibly at a gist in case there are
> additional updates?)
>
>
> On Mon, Sep 12, 2016 at 12:19 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Thanks for all the suggestions! (Down to 8 minutes, and more than
>> twice as many effective samples.) Updated versions attached.
>>
>> 1) Moving the random number generation to R instead of transformed
>> data is important as there's now much better convergence of the
>> different chains, which makes sense since they're actually using the
>> same features now. But before you go and fix this, might be worth
>> seeing what other people use it for...I could imagine the current
>> behavior of different seeds for transformed data making sense in some
>> cases.
>>
>> 2) OK, good to hear about unary function vectorization. I guess I was
>> hoping that analytic gradients would make a big difference in terms of
>> the shared computations you're talking about. Consider n = 1 so we
>> have a real x, a parameter bw we want to learn, and omega is a vector
>> of size k. If sin(.) was vectorized, then we'd have:
>>
>> sinfeatures = sin(omega * bw * x);
>>
>> and the gradient with respect to x would be:
>>
>> (omega * bw) .* cos(omega * bw * x)
>>
>> i.e. elementwise product of two vectors. (For n > 1 it's elementwise
>> product of two matrices.) Won't that be faster since omega * bw will
>> only need to be calculated once?
>>
>> Seth
>>
>> On Mon, Sep 12, 2016 at 3:17 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>> > We'll have all the unary functions vectorized soon, but there
>> > won't be any speedup over loops because there are no shared
>> > computations. We might be able to get fancier with the implementation
>> > and cut down some virtual function calls, but that's minor compared
>> > to shared computations.
>> >
>> > But you can speed up this loop:
>> >
>> > for(i in 1:n)
>> > for(j in 1:k) {
>> > cosfeatures[i,j] = scale * cos(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
>> > sinfeatures[i,j] = scale * sin(omega[j] * bw * x[i]);
>> > }
>> >
>> > Define the I x J matrix of omega * x, then multpily it by bw,
>> > then use it to define cosfeatures and sinfeatures without the
>> > scale, then multiply through by the scale.
>> >
>> > The target+= forms of the densities are slower than the
>> > ~ forms because they don't drop constant terms (yes, yes, versions
>> > that do drop constants are on my to-do list buried somewhere I
>> > might get to them next year if I'm lucky).
>> >
>> > With transformed data now, different RNGs get used per chain.
>> > I'm going to fix that for the next release.
>> >
>> > It'll also be faster if you only save fhat as a transformed parameter
>> > and use that in the last normal_lpdf --- less I/O per iteration (reduces
>> > n x k to n) and also saves some redundant calculations in generated
>> > quantities.
>> >
>> > sqrt(2.0 / n) rather than sqrt(2 / (1.0 * n)) just for clarity.
>> >
>> > - Bob
>> >
>> >> On Sep 12, 2016, at 8:39 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >>
>> >> Hi all.
>> >>
>> >> Attached are two examples of using random Fourier features
>> >> [Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximate Gaussian process regression.
>> >> The idea is that the covariance matrix is approximated by an explicit
>> >> randomized feature expansion of the kernel. With an explicit feature
>> >> space expansion, there's no costly multivariate matrix algebra--it
>> >> just becomes Bayesian linear regression on the new features.
>> >>
>> >> In rff1.stan, I don't learn the lengthscale and it's very fast for
>> >> 1000 data points. In rff2.stan, I do learn the lengthscale and it's
>> >> pretty slow (10 minutes), though it can still handle 1000 data points
>> >> with a small number of features. (Note that in the attached I only
>> >> have 10 features, but in real applications people often use 10K-100K
>> >> features!)
>> >>
>> >> Anyone have thoughts on speeding up rff2.stan? My guess is that
>> >> there'd be a big speedup from a vectorized sin/cos, with analytic
>> >> gradients. If that sounds right, I'll file a feature request and
>> >> hopefully Rob and I can tackle this (+ anyone else who wants to help).
>> >>
>> >> Seth
>> >>
